title: Support diversified route and product development

blocks.text: 3.2.2 Product and destination capacity

The second supply theme covers what visitors find once they arrive: product beyond the icons, the quality of the stay and the limits of the flagship sites. The three focus areas work as a set. New product gives visitors a reason to travel outward, quality standards make that product safe to sell and flow management at the flagships sends the overflow to it.
Theme 2.2 · Product and destination capacity · Focus area 10
Support diversified route and product development

The province does not lack attractions; it lacks finished experiences around them, with assets outside the Metro left without guides, interpretation or bookable product and one touring route of six rated Ready.
The challenge

The growth case needs visitors to travel beyond the Cape Peninsula, stay longer and spend in more places. The province has the assets to support that. Of 50,332 mapped tourism assets, the Cape Metro holds 40.3% and the five other districts the rest (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p2, p23). The West Coast has the highest natural-asset attractiveness in the province and the Central Karoo its most unique niche assets (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p88).

Yet both score lowest on readiness, and the product around the assets is unfinished (section 2.3). Eleven of 16 organisations engaged see the offer as concentrated around Cape Town and a narrow set of icons (Stakeholder Insights Report, Mar 2026, p11; the count is reconstructed from the appendix tables). The Department of Economic Development adds that destination development has focused more on managing barriers than on building product outside the Cape Peninsula (Stakeholder Insights Report, Mar 2026, p24).

Nine of the ten places international tourists visit most are in the Metro (Provincial Economic Review and Outlook 2025, p68). That concentration costs the province twice. The flagships run full in season while the township attractions are underused (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p24). Further out, strong product sits where visitors cannot easily reach or afford it (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p89).

blocks.message: Assets are spread across the province, but product, packaging and investment stop at the core routes.

blocks.text: The evidence locates the constraint. It is less about creating new attractions and more about turning existing assets into complete, accessible visitor experiences (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p114). Each route falls short on something different: accommodation and bookability on the West Coast, bookability on Route 62 and depth beyond Hermanus on the Whale Coast (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p62, p73, p84). The Winelands and the Garden Route fall short only on safety (section 2.3).

No committed capital yet follows the gap (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p54, p76). No source counts the assets that have no product around them [assets with no bookable product or guided access, by district: needs the Wesgro supply database behind the 50,332 count]. The first design task is therefore to size the gap district by district.
The course of action

Wesgro works outward from strength. The Garden Route, the Cape Winelands and the Overberg already have strong underlying product and need connectivity, packaging and service depth (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p114). Route 62 and the West Coast are packaged as slow-travel products. In 2027 and 2028 the Tourism unit designs bookable itineraries for all six touring routes. Delivery starts from 2029 on the Garden Route, the Cape Winelands and the Overberg, which are closest to ready. It moves to Route 62 and the West Coast once their product is online (focus area 3; section 4.3).

The City is a natural partner. Its framework for 2019 to 2024 proposed a Cape Town+ offer linking the city with the surrounding regions (City of Cape Town, Tourism Development Framework 2019 to 2024, p5). Stellenbosch and George can anchor regional business events, which gives the Convention Bureau a part to play (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p41). The capital sits with others. Accommodation investors and municipalities add beds and service depth in secondary towns later in the period (focus area 15). SANParks carries the precinct projects, and rural broadband sits with national government (focus area 3).

blocks.text: Why it can work

The actions supply what the assets lack: a guide, a bed and a booking route. Packaging turns scattered assets into a trip a visitor can buy, and a multi-day itinerary gives a reason to stay outside the Metro. The Overberg shows both the pull and the limit. Its whale-watching anchor sustains operator confidence despite flat accessibility, yet De Hoop still lacks accommodation investment and year-round product is unfunded (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p75, p76).

Chile ran Santiago, Valparaíso, the wine valleys and Patagonia as one portfolio. It reports longer stays and shoulder-season revenue from the approach, though no figure is printed for either (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p27). The change for the Western Cape is to sell experiences as curated journeys and move from asset marketing to experience-led packaging (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p28). The condition is that the other entries keep pace. Itineraries sell only if the product can be booked (focus area 3), reached without a car (focus area 9) and stayed in. Without beds, a packaged route stays a day trip from Cape Town.
